items.title: Enquiry triage and routing
items.problem: Enquiries arrive as free text across WhatsApp, email and the web form. The details — who, what, how urgent, which order — are re-read by a human every time, and the reply goes out late because the reply depends on reading carefully.
items.approach: A deterministic rules engine parses the raw message into a structured record: sender and business, intent with a confidence score and runner-up, urgency with the phrases that triggered it, extracted order references, budget and timeline, the gaps still missing, a routing decision with an SLA, and a reply draft for a human to approve.
items.outcome: The same record, every time, in under a second — with every classification traceable to the phrase that produced it.

items.title: Rapid AI Opportunity Audit
items.problem: A business knows something is slow, but not where the time actually goes, and does not want to commit to a project before seeing the size of the prize.
items.approach: A fixed-scope diagnostic: we map the operational friction, rank automation candidates by impact against effort, recommend tooling and a sequence, and state plainly which parts are not worth changing.
items.outcome: A written memo in 72 hours that the owner keeps whether or not they work with us — priced at PKR 3,000 with no obligation to continue.

items.title: Website design system
items.problem: Teams rebuild the same page over and over because nothing is written down, and every new page looks slightly different from the last.
items.approach: Tokens for colour, type scale, spacing and radii; component patterns with documented states; responsive behaviour defined per breakpoint; and a token file that a developer can pick up and use.
items.outcome: New pages that match by default, and a design system that survives the person who made it.

items.title: Automation opportunity model
items.problem: Every business wants automation, and most automation proposals are written by vendors who benefit from saying yes. Ranking is usually done on excitement, not on numbers.
items.approach: The client enters their own hours, cost and error rates. The model converts those into annual hours recovered, annual benefit, build effort and a payback period, then sorts the work into four quadrants — including the quadrant labelled “leave alone”.
items.outcome: A defensible shortlist, including the work that should be left alone — which is the part most proposals leave out.

items.title: Reference system architecture
items.problem: Systems get built one workflow at a time, so the third automation fights the first, and nothing documents the whole picture.
items.approach: Five layers — capture, route, automate, document, review — each with the components we implement, the signals we measure, the tools we usually reach for and the failure modes we design against.
items.outcome: A target architecture a business can be held to, and a gap analysis against where it actually is today.

items.title: Scope brief builder
items.problem: Most bad projects are bad briefs. The client describes a symptom, the quote prices a guess, and the first invoice is where the misunderstanding surfaces.
items.approach: Eight structured questions capture the friction, the volume, the tools, the business impact, the timeline and the budget band — then the model routes the brief, estimates a duration and generates a written brief that can be sent as-is.
items.outcome: Both sides start from the same document, which is where a project stops being a guess.
